newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian foreign minister to be nominated for PM.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian foreign minister to be nominated for PM.

text.p: A dissident faction of ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party said on Wednesday it would nominate Cambodian Foreign Minister Ung Huot as the prince's replacement.
The leader of the faction, Toan Chay, who had been tipped to replace Ranariddh as strongman Hun Sen's co-premier, told reporters he could not take the job because he was not a member of parliament.

"We have already proposed Ung Huot to be prime minister, we completely agree with each other," Toan Chay told reporters, referring to his dissident faction and the remainder of Ranariddh's royalist party in the country.

Second Prime Minister Hun Sen overthrew Ranariddh on July 6 but said he wanted the coalition between his Cambodian People's Party and FUNCINPEC to remain in place and for the royalist party to choose a new first prime minister to replace Ranariddh.
Toan Chay said the name of Ung Huot, who returned to Phnom Penh from France on Monday, would be forwarded to the National Assembly when it reopened later this month.
Toan Chay said he could not be first prime minister because the constitution required the post be filled by a member of parliament.
"I can't accept the premiership because...I am not a member of parliament. I am only the governor of a province, and His Majesty the King asked that the constitution not be amended," he said.
Toan Chay, the governor of Siem Reap province who broke with Ranariddh in April, said Ung Huot had agreed to become first prime minister.
"This is very good because Ung Huot is considered to be a neutral person who we trust with our destiny over the next year," he said, referring to Cambodia's next election due in May.
Many FUNCINPEC members left the country in the aftermath of Ranariddh's ouster and the killing of at least two senior party officials.

Ranariddh, who left the country the day before Hun Sen's forces moved against the prince's troops in the capital, has called for resistance to Hun Sen and appealed to the international community for support.

The prince has pleaded his case in meetings with French and Japanese envoys in Paris, U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan in New York, and U.S. State Department officials and members of Congress in Washington, as well as in telephone calls from the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN).
But apart from a sympathetic hearing and advice to try to make peace with Hun Sen, the prince has received no firm offers of support.
